verifyText.value: Basics of renter's insurance

While your landlord's insurance covers the building in which you live, you should buy a separate policy to cover your possessions if you rent. The provisions of a renters' policy are nearly identical to those of a homeowner's policy. You are protected against loss or damage from the most common perils, such as fire, explosion, water damage, vandalism, or theft. If you own valuables, jewelry, computers and, other valuable items, you probably need a rider to provide coverage beyond the typical limits.

Taking inventory

Take a household inventory to see what actually needs to be insured. Walk around your home and list on an inventory sheet each item you own, what you paid for it and how much it might cost to replace. Also note model and serial numbers. If you have no idea what things cost today, you might consider bringing in an appraiser to help you.

In addition to listing your household possessions, photograph or videotape each room. If you videotape, talk about the objects you are taping and estimate how much they cost. Keep the pictures or video somewhere other than your home, such as at work so you will have access to it if your house is destroyed or damaged. These physical records can be invaluable if you ever file a claim and need to convince an adjuster that you owned a particular item and what that item is worth.
Protecting your valuables
Most renters' policies impose a $1,500 limit on jewelry, $3,000 to $10,000 on computers, and $2,500 to $10,000 on silverware.
As with homeowner's insurance, it is best to buy replacement cost coverage rather than a policy based on current cash value.
Roommates

If you rent an apartment with several roommates, many companies write policies allowing you to cover all the contents of your apartment, no matter to whom they belong. If you get a new roommate, you will probably have to tell the insurance company and list his or her name on the policy.

Unmarried couples living together can also obtain coverage if it is specifically allowed in the policy. Some policies automatically extend coverage to any future resident of a policyholder's household that is considered a domestic partner.
Covering liability

In addition to property coverage, most renters' policies provide liability insurance to cover you if someone claims injury due to your negligence. For example, bodily injury liability pays medical costs, as well as your legal defense fees, if you accidentally injure or kill someone.
Keeping your premiums down
Renter's insurance is not that expensive but you can shave your premium payments:
If you go with the company that carries your auto policy.
If you accept a higher deductible.
Filing a claim

If your property sustains damage or if you suffer a property loss, report it to your insurance agent immediately. Take pictures of any damage as soon as possible in case the insurance adjuster cannot examine the scene right away. Also report thefts or burglaries to the police at once because your insurance agent will request a police report in order to investigate your claim.
Damage report checklist
If theft or burglary, call the police at once.
Get a copy of the police report for your insurance agent.
Call agent to report damage or loss.
Determine if policy covers damage or loss.
Claim exceeds deductible.
Ask how long claim will take to process.
Ask what the procedure is for getting estimates to repair or replace items damaged or lost.
Follow up phone conversation with letter detailing damage or loss.
If necessary, make temporary repairs to prevent further damage and submit receipts for reimbursement.
Contesting the settlement

If you disagree with the settlement your insurance company is offering, ask your agent for an explanation. You do not have to accept an agent's first offer. Often, he or she will negotiate the settlement with you until you are satisfied. If your agent still does not offer what you think you deserve after such negotiations or if your claim was rejected, you:

Send a copy of your original letter initiating the claim as well as a new letter explaining your dispute to the chief claims officer at the executive office of your insurance company. All reputable companies have internal investigation departments to help resolve disputes.

Complain to your state insurance department. (For a complete list of state insurance regulators, visit the National Association of Insurance Commissioners web site). All insurance companies are regulated, and the insurance department should be able to help you if it agrees with your complaint.

Have an independent arbitrator decide whether the settlement offer is fair. Your insurance company may be able to recommend such an arbitrator through Arbitration Forums, Inc. (3820 Northdale Blvd., Tampa, FL 33624; (866) 977-3434), that supplies insurance arbitration specialists. You may also be able to obtain an arbitrator on your own through the American Arbitration Association (120 Broadway, Floor 21, New York, NY 10271; (800) 778-7879).
Legal issues

When all else fails, hire a lawyer and sue the insurance company to collect a fair settlement. This process could cost hundreds or thousands of dollars and take many months or even years of litigation. Therefore, your claim must be substantial enough to make all of this trouble worthwhile. Your lawyer should also give you an honest opinion about your odds of winning the case.
